blocks.text: …pay the four months of back rent you owe. Otherwise, this notice stands."
His sneer disappeared. He picked up the notice, read it twice, and set it down very carefully.

I hadn't known about the back rent until Saturday, when the attorneys walked me through my grandfather's files. My manager, Brian, hadn't paid rent since July. Every month, he sent an email blaming slow sales. And every month, my grandfather quietly wrote back, "Take another month." In the margin of one letter, Grandpa had written in pencil: "Twelve people work there. Don't punish them for him."
That was who my grandfather was. It was also why I wasn't there to get revenge. I was there to follow the lease.
"You can't do this because I fired you," Brian said.
"I'm not," I said. "I'm doing it because you owe fifty-two thousand dollars.
Your lease allows the landlord to terminate after sixty days of nonpayment. My grandfather gave you a hundred and twenty."

He didn't pay by five o'clock. He couldn't. But the franchise wasn't really his to lose. It belonged to a national chain, and his franchise agreement required him to stay current on rent. When I called their regional office, they were very interested to hear he'd been in default for four months. They removed him as franchisee within the week.

The chain brought in a new franchise owner, a woman who'd managed three of their other locations. She paid the back rent as part of taking over and signed a new lease. She kept all twelve employees. Her first policy change was three days of paid bereavement leave for every employee, no questions asked.
She offered me my old job back, with a promotion.
I thanked her and said no. I'm busy learning how to manage three buildings now. But I stop by the store every Friday, and the staff always save me a coffee.
My grandfather's photo hangs in the lobby of the plaza now. Under it, I put a small brass plaque with the note he wrote in that margin.
